paragraphs.heading: Carrying pollen
paragraphs.text: Pollination is the movement of pollen from a plant's anther to a stigma, which later allows fertilisation and the making of seeds. Many agents carry pollen: insects such as bees, beetles and butterflies, as well as birds, bats, water, wind and even plants themselves. Animals that go from plant to plant carry pollen on their bodies. In doing so they move genetic material that most flowering plants need in order to reproduce.

paragraphs.heading: Self, cross and hybrid
paragraphs.text: Self-pollination can happen inside a closed flower or between flowers of one plant. Pollination often stays within a species, but when it crosses between species it can produce hybrid offspring, both in nature and in plant breeding. It matters for farming and gardening because fruiting depends on fertilisation, which pollination makes possible.

paragraphs.heading: Double fertilisation
paragraphs.text: In flowering plants, a pollen grain that lands on the stigma germinates and sends a pollen tube down the style to an ovary. Its two gametes travel down the tube and enter an ovule through the micropyle, a pore at the tip of the ovule. One male nucleus joins the egg cell to make the embryo, and the other fuses with the polar bodies to make endosperm tissue. Because of these two fusions the process is called double fertilisation, and it yields a seed holding both nourishing tissue and an embryo.

paragraphs.heading: Waking the pollen
paragraphs.text: Pollen germination happens in three stages: hydration, activation and the emergence of the pollen tube. The grain is badly dried out, which cuts its mass and makes it easier to carry between flowers. It germinates only after it takes up water again, so it does not start too early inside the anther. Water lets its membrane re-form into a working osmotic barrier, and activation builds actin filaments that gather where the tube will push out.

paragraphs.heading: Pollination in conifers
paragraphs.text: Gymnosperms do it differently: their ovules sit exposed on a support such as a cone scale, not inside a carpel. In conifers, the reproductive parts are carried on cones, either male pollen cones or female ovulate cones. Wind carries pollen grains to the female cone, and a grain landing near the tip of an ovule is often drawn in through the micropyle by a drop of liquid called a pollination drop. There it may wait a year before growing a pollen tube, which finally delivers sperm to the female gametophyte, where one sperm nucleus enters the egg cell.

paragraphs.heading: Swimming sperm and the science
paragraphs.text: Gymnosperms reach the egg in one of two ways. Cycads and Ginkgo have sperm that swim straight to the egg inside the ovule, while conifers and gnetophytes have sperm that cannot swim and are carried along a pollen tube. The study of pollination spans botany, horticulture, entomology and ecology, and pollination by insects has its own name, anthecology. Christian Konrad Sprengel first treated pollination as an interaction between flower and carrier, in the 18th century.
